disclaimer: A score is an evidence-based judgment, not a verdict. It is an estimate from the evidence found, never proof of intent.

factors.label: Sourcing
factors.description: Anonymous or circular sources, no primary document, single-source claim.

factors.label: Verifiability
factors.description: Can the core fact be independently confirmed? Does a second independent source confirm it?

factors.label: Framing and language
factors.description: Loaded words, headline that contradicts the body, emotional trigger words.

factors.label: Omission and context
factors.description: Key facts, dates, denominators or counter-claims left out; old material presented as new.

factors.label: Emotional manipulation
factors.description: Fear, outrage or tribal-identity hooks doing more work than facts.

factors.label: Amplification pattern
factors.description: Identical wording across outlets or accounts, sudden coordinated push, timing that serves an obvious beneficiary.

factors.label: Source incentive
factors.description: Who gains if you believe this, and is that party the source?

method_note: Every sourced psyop found in a week is scored and listed under that week; a story with no sourced, openable evidence is not scored. The score applies to the claim named in 'scored claim', not to the outlet's reporting of it: where the Outlet column shows a fact-checker or news outlet, the claim being scored is often the viral post, video or official statement it examined. Honest note on skew: the scores in this data run high. 176 of 222 psyops (79%) score 5 to 9, the mean is 6.1, and 7 is the most common score (65). Many of the high scores belong to viral fakes and AI-generated items that fact-checkers had already debunked, and the scan favored stories with a checkable claim, so this is a selected sample, not a base rate for the news. The skew was noted and no score was altered. Eight psyops carry a confidence label of 'Medium-High' as recorded by the scan. Weeks that are in progress or not yet scanned stay in this file and are not shown.

psyops.headline: Judge temporarily blocks Trump's effort to deploy national guard in Chicago
psyops.scored_claim: The administration's factual account, in three government declarations, that violent protests at the Broadview ICE facility justified federalizing and deploying National Guard troops in Illinois.
psyops.selection_reason: Court record directly tests the government's factual account; Reuters, Guardian, BBC and Al Jazeera cover the ruling in-window.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: Only three declarants with first-hand knowledge of Illinois events were offered, and the court wrote that 'all three contain unreliable information' (Opinion, Doc. 70, p.11).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: The court could not reconcile the declarations with accounts from state and local law enforcement and wrote it 'cannot conclude that Defendants' declarations are reliable'. Most photos of protesters 'wearing gas masks' showed Covid-19 masks (Doc. 70, n.5).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: The court noted a 'troubling trend of Defendants' declarants equating protests with riots'. Al Jazeera describes the 'war zone' depiction of Chicago as false; that is the outlet's characterization.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The declarations cited 9/27 arrests of people allegedly carrying weapons but did not disclose that federal grand juries declined to indict at least three of them (Doc. 70, p.10). A declaration saying the FPS had requested Guard support for the federal courthouse was inaccurate and later corrected (Doc. 62-3, Doc. 65-1).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Trump's earlier public statements about Chicago quoted in the opinion's footnote ('carnage', 'I'll straighten it out') are fear and threat framings, but the declarations themselves are mostly dry factual statements.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Similar declarations by the same officials were filed in Chicago Headline Club v. Noem (Doc. 70, p.10), so the same account was reused across cases. No coordination beyond that is shown.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: The government is the source and the litigant, and gains deference from courts if the facts show a 'rebellion' or inability to execute the laws. The court gave no deference on what counts as rebellion.

target_audience.text: Federal judges, who must find a factual predicate under 10 U.S.C. 12406; secondarily a domestic audience receptive to a 'violent city' narrative.

confidence.reason: I read the 51-page opinion directly from CourtListener. Guardian, Al Jazeera and BBC agree on the ruling. The findings are at the temporary restraining order stage and are disputed by the government.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: the government's declarations omitted that grand juries refused to indict at least three of the 9/27 arrestees, and one declaration misstated a request for Guard support. The court found the declarants' perceptions unreliable.
psyops.summary: On 10/9 and 10/10 Judge April Perry temporarily blocked the deployment, finding the government's declarations unreliable and no factual basis for a 'danger of rebellion'. The score applies to the government's factual account, not to outlets' accurate reporting of the ruling.
psyops.counter_argument: The court wrote that it 'does not doubt that there have been acts of vandalism, civil disobedience, and even assaults on federal agents', and the ruling is preliminary. The government argues it needs troops to protect federal officers and property (BBC, Reuters).
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented, not knowable on 10/9-10/12): on 10/22 the order was extended indefinitely by agreement, and Capitol News Illinois reports a 7th Circuit panel wrote that 'political opposition is not rebellion'.
gaps: The government's declarations (Docs. 62-1 to 62-4) were not opened; they are described through the court's opinion.
Reuters original returned HTTP 401 (paywall/blocked) and was not read.
The DHS account of events at Broadview was not independently verified on the ground.

psyops.headline: White House blasts Nobel Committee for not awarding Peace Prize to Trump
psyops.scored_claim: White House communications director Steven Cheung's statement that 'The Nobel Committee proved they place politics over peace.'
psyops.selection_reason: Named official's characterization of a committee's motive, reported across wire, US and foreign outlets on 10/10.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The statement is on-the-record, from a named official, posted on X and quoted by BBC, CNBC, Reuters and NYT.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: A claim about the committee's motive cannot be tested. The chair said the committee bases its decision 'only on the work and the will of Alfred Nobel' (CNBC).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Politics over peace' casts the committee as political without evidence, while Trump had openly campaigned for the prize (NYT, CNBC).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: NYT notes Secretary of State Rubio signed a letter to the Nobel Committee supporting Machado's nomination, which the statement leaves out. [NYT page returned HTTP 403; this is from its search excerpt.]

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Grievance framing ('snub'), and Trump reposted a video of Putin saying the award 'has lost credibility' (BBC).

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Trump reshared Machado's dedication and the Putin clip within hours (BBC). This reads as an amplification push around one narrative.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: The source is the spokesman of the person who lobbied for the prize and gains if the result looks illegitimate (BBC, Reuters).

target_audience.text: Trump's domestic base and supporters, and international observers who might read the Nobel Committee as partisan.

confidence.reason: BBC and CNBC were opened and agree; Reuters (HTTP 401) and NYT (HTTP 403) were not opened and are read from search excerpts. Cheung's X post was not opened.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: the claim attributes a political motive to the committee without evidence, while the speaker's principal had campaigned for the prize and posted a Putin clip calling the award not credible.
psyops.summary: On 10/10 María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize. The White House said the committee put 'politics over peace'. Machado dedicated the prize partly to Trump. A senior official told CBS that Trump called her to congratulate her (BBC). The score applies to the motive claim, not to outlets' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: A spokesman's reaction to losing an award he openly sought is ordinary partisan spin and carries no factual claim beyond opinion. Trump himself did not directly criticize the committee when asked that evening (Reuters excerpt), and Rubio backed Machado (NYT excerpt).
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window, none checked; outcome of the story is the prize itself, not testable later.
gaps: Cheung's X post was not opened; it is quoted by BBC, CNBC and Reuters identically.
Reuters (HTTP 401) and NYT (HTTP 403) were blocked; their text was taken from search excerpts only.
The committee's deliberations are confidential, so the motive claim cannot be checked.
Reuters link (https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/white-house-says-nobel-committee-places-politics-over-peace-2025-10-10/) returned HTTP 401 on 2026-10-16; not independently opened.
The New York Times link (https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/10/us/politics/nobel-trump-rubio-venezuela.html) returned HTTP 403 on 2026-10-16; not independently opened.

psyops.headline: Israel and Hamas agree first phase of Gaza ceasefire deal
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's 10/8 Truth Social announcement that 'Israel and Hamas have both signed off on the first Phase of our Peace Plan' and that 'ALL of the Hostages will be released very soon.'
psyops.selection_reason: Plain, high-salience event with a primary statement and independent confirmation from both parties; included as a low-score baseline.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The announcement is a primary statement by the President (Truth Social 10/8 6:51 PM EDT, also in the Daily Compilation of Presidential Documents).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Hamas confirmed the agreement (BBC, Anadolu), and Israel's cabinet ratified it early 10/9 (Al Jazeera).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: Capitalized, celebratory language ('GREAT Day', 'Historic and Unprecedented Event', 'BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS').

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The post says nothing about what was left unresolved. BBC notes Hamas disarmament and Gaza governance are still to be negotiated and a January ceasefire had collapsed after two months.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Celebratory, but no fear or outrage hook doing more work than the facts.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: No identical-wording push beyond normal reposting.

incentive.label: documented incentive
incentive.note: Trump is the source and gains credit, and was openly seeking the Nobel Peace Prize (BBC, CNBC, 10/10).

target_audience.text: n/a (plain news with a mild self-credit frame). Secondary audience, inference: U.S. voters and foreign leaders watching Trump's diplomacy.

confidence.reason: Primary statement read at govinfo.gov, with BBC, Al Jazeera and Anadolu agreeing on the facts. Phase-one details came from officials and anonymous sources quoted by BBC.

psyops.summary: Trump announced on 10/8 that both sides accepted phase one of his plan. Hamas and Israel confirmed. Details such as maps and prisoner lists were reported through officials and anonymous sources.
psyops.counter_argument: None of substance; the main counter-point is that 'ALL of the Hostages' includes deceased hostages whose return was still uncertain (Al Jazeera notes 48 captives, about 20 alive).
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (not knowable on 10/8): a Denver Clarion weekly summary reports Hamas released 20 living hostages on 10/13 in exchange for about 2,000 Palestinian prisoners. I did not open a primary report of the release for this entry.
gaps: The BBC article relies partly on anonymous 'sources told the BBC' for the terms.
The Anadolu timestamp has no time zone; treated as 10/9 local.
The Truth Social post itself was read through govinfo.gov and trumpstruth.org, not truthsocial.com.

psyops.headline: Fact-checking President Donald Trump's claims about peace, war and Iran after his Israel address
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's 10/13 Knesset claim: 'we settled eight wars in eight months', and that U.S. bombs 'totally' obliterated Iran's nuclear facilities, 'confirmed'.
psyops.selection_reason: Recurring talking point checked by fact-checkers the same day; a primary transcript is available.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The claim is on the record in the transcript (American Presidency Project). No list of the eight wars is given in the speech itself.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Poynter/PolitiFact: the 'eight wars' talking point is 'exaggerated'. Violence continued after the Congo-Rwanda deal; Cambodia and Thailand traded ceasefire-violation accusations; Egypt-Ethiopia is a diplomatic dispute; for Kosovo-Serbia there is 'little evidence' war was brewing. On Iran, 'impossible to know' whether the sites were 'obliterated' (Al Jazeera text of the same fact-check).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Settled' and 'obliterated' are absolute words for incremental or unverified outcomes.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The claim leaves out that several deals were temporary or disputed by other leaders, and that no public damage assessment of the Iran strikes exists (Poynter, Al Jazeera).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Triumphal tone ('It feels so good to say it'), but no fear or outrage hook doing the main work.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: PolitiFact calls it a 'repeated talking point'. Trump repeats it often, and said in the same speech that he had said seven the day before.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: The speaker is the beneficiary of the claim, in a speech made as he sought the Nobel Peace Prize (BBC, 10/10).

target_audience.text: Trump's domestic base and a foreign audience (Israeli Knesset, Gulf and Nobel-watching audiences) that rewards the peacemaker image.

confidence.reason: I read the transcript and the Poynter, PolitiFact and Al Jazeera fact-check texts. The Al Jazeera piece reproduces the Poynter/PolitiFact text, so it is not an independent check. The AP fact-check returned HTTP 403.

psyops.summary: In his 10/13 Knesset speech Trump said he had 'settled eight wars in eight months' and that the Iran strikes 'totally' obliterated its nuclear sites. Fact-checkers rated the war count exaggerated and the Iran damage unverifiable. The Gaza deal he was celebrating that day was real. The score applies to the claims, not to outlets' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Trump did play a role in several ceasefires (Israel-Iran, India-Pakistan, Armenia-Azerbaijan) and the Gaza deal is a landmark (Poynter). 'Settled' may be read as shorthand for brokering. Intelligence assessments of the Iran strikes may say more than public sources show.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window: not checked in this entry.
gaps: The AP fact-check ('Trump claims he's ended eight wars...') returned HTTP 403 and was not read.
Al Jazeera republished the Poynter/PolitiFact text, so only one independent fact-check chain was read.
No classified or public damage assessment of the Iran strikes was available.

psyops.headline: MAGA-world already blaming 'Antifa' boogeyman for upcoming No Kings protests
psyops.scored_claim: Statements by administration officials and Republican leaders that the 10/18 'No Kings' protests were a 'Hate America' rally run by Antifa, paid protesters and the 'pro-Hamas wing' (Duffy 10/13, Emmer and Bondi 10/14; Johnson and Marshall 10/10).
psyops.selection_reason: Same label repeated by at least five named officials in one week, with fact-based counter-evidence available from the event itself.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: Duffy: 'it begs the question who's funding it'. Johnson: 'It's being told to us'. Emmer: 'The rumor is'. None offered a document or named source (Independent, Media Matters).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: The organizing coalition is led by Indivisible with groups including the ACLU and League of Women Voters (Media Matters; Independent says none is tied to antifa networks). Antifa is a movement, not an organization (Wray testimony quoted by Media Matters). BBC reported the 10/18 events as peaceful, with NYPD reporting no protest-related arrests.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Hate America' rally, 'pro-Hamas wing', 'terrorist wing' of the Democratic Party (Independent). Protesters said 'We're not here because we hate America' (BBC).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The claims leave out the mainstream coalition behind the events and that June's No Kings protests were largely peaceful with few arrests (Independent). Trump's 'antifa' designation and NSPM-7 context is described by Media Matters.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Tribal and fear hooks: 'rabid base', 'hate for America', 'paid anarchists' (Independent, Media Matters).

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Media Matters lists the same 'Hate America' / antifa / paid-protester framing from Johnson (10/10), Marshall (10/10), Duffy (10/13), Emmer (10/14) and Bondi (10/14), on Fox and Newsmax, within five days. Media Matters is an advocacy group; I confirmed the Duffy, Johnson and Emmer quotes in the Independent.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: The officials framed the rally as the reason Democrats would not end the shutdown, and Trump allies were building a case for NSPM-7 and Guard deployments (Independent, Media Matters). The speakers are the source and the beneficiary.

target_audience.text: Republican base and Fox/Newsmax audiences, and swing voters being steered to blame Democrats for the shutdown; secondary target is protest organizers and funders facing possible investigation.

confidence.reason: Quotes confirmed in two outlets (Independent, Media Matters) and BBC's account of the rally itself. I did not open the Fox, Newsmax or Hannity clips.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: the same 'Hate America' / antifa / paid-protester framing was repeated by at least five named officials in five days without evidence, while the shutdown was in its third week. The 10/18 events were peaceful, per BBC and the NYPD figure it quotes.
psyops.summary: From 10/10 to 10/14 Republican leaders and cabinet officials described the planned 10/18 No Kings protests as an antifa and 'Hate America' event. Organizers called it a nonviolent mainstream coalition. The score applies to the claims, not to outlets' accurate reporting of them.
psyops.counter_argument: Antifa-linked violence at some 2025 protests is a real subject of dispute, and Trump described specific attacks on law enforcement at his antifa event (Media Matters). Coalition groups are funded by foundations and donors, and 'paid' could be argued on that basis (inference). No evidence was offered for the 'paid' claim.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window: not checked. Within the window, BBC reported nearly seven million attendees by organizers' count and that the events were peaceful.
gaps: Fox Business, Fox News, Newsmax and Hannity original interviews were not opened.
The Hill's article returned HTTP 403 and was not read.
Attendance figures come from organizers (BBC), not an independent count.
Media Matters is an advocacy organization and was used only for quotes also confirmed elsewhere or attributed to named officials.

psyops.headline: News outlets including The New York Times and Newsmax say they won't sign Pentagon rules document
psyops.scored_claim: Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell's claim that the new press policy is 'common sense media procedures' that 'does not ask for them to agree, just to acknowledge', and Hegseth's 'yes' to a follower's framing that reporters just want unrestricted roaming of the Pentagon.
psyops.selection_reason: Official characterization contrasted with the rule text as described by AP, and with a near-unanimous refusal by outlets including a pro-Trump network.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: Parnell and Hegseth spoke on the record (AP text via PBS).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: AP describes rules that bar unescorted access to large parts of the building and let Hegseth revoke credentials for asking anyone for information 'that he has not approved for release'. That conflicts with the portrayal as mere acknowledgment. I did not open the policy text itself.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Full blown meltdown, crying victim online' and a hand-waving emoji replying to the Times' statement (AP text).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The statements leave out that acknowledgment is a condition of credentials and that soliciting unapproved unclassified information is grounds for revocation (AP text). Reporters say neither of Hegseth's follower-question assertions is true.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Mocking tone and a 'classified military installation under the First Amendment' framing invites tribal reaction.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Hegseth reposted a follower's question and answered 'yes' in the same news cycle; Parnell's lines were echoed across outlets, but no wider coordinated push was shown.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: The Pentagon is the source and gains control of information if the policy is seen as a harmless procedure.

target_audience.text: Trump-aligned audiences receptive to a 'press as adversary' frame; also the outlets themselves, who are pressed to comply.

confidence.reason: The AP text via PBS was opened and quotes both officials. I could not open the policy memo, Reuters (HTTP 401) or Axios (HTTP 403) coverage, so the rule text is known only from AP's description.

psyops.summary: On 10/13 the Times, AP, Reuters, the Post and Newsmax said they would not sign the Pentagon's press-policy acknowledgment. Parnell said the policy asked only for acknowledgment. Reporters said it punishes routine newsgathering. The score applies to the officials' characterization, not to the outlets' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: The Pentagon has real classified-information concerns, and Parnell said the policy was revised to clarify that reporters need not submit writing for approval (The Hill excerpt). The officials' point that acknowledgment is not agreement has some textual support. One outlet, One America News, signed (Reuters excerpt).
psyops.hindsight_note: Within the week, per Reuters and Axios headlines, reporters turned in badges and vacated the Pentagon on 10/15. I could not open either article, so this is headline-level.
gaps: The Pentagon policy memo was not opened. A 9/19 memo and later revision exist; only AP's description was read.
Reuters returned HTTP 401 and Axios HTTP 403.
The Hill revision article returned HTTP 403 and is cited only from a search excerpt.

psyops.headline: Trump told Zelenskyy he'd try to end the war 'on the current line' in difficult White House meeting
psyops.scored_claim: The Financial Times account, relayed by POLITICO and Reuters, that the 10/17 Trump-Zelenskyy meeting became a shouting match with Trump 'cursing all the time' and tossing aside frontline maps.
psyops.selection_reason: Anonymous-source account of a closed meeting, with a named dispute inside the reporting.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: Everything about the meeting comes from unnamed people: FT 'several sources', and two anonymous people to POLITICO.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: POLITICO's source says 'Trump did not toss any war maps. He just said he was tired of different maps'. An EU diplomat said the meeting was 'not as bleak as reported'. The core outcome ('try to end this on the current line') is confirmed by POLITICO's source.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Shouting match' and 'cursing all the time' are vivid, with echoes of the February meeting.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Public statements by Trump after the meeting (Putin 'wants to end the war') were not in the FT account as POLITICO summarizes it.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Humiliation and conflict imagery attracts attention beyond the policy substance.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Several outlets ran the FT-sourced account within 48 hours (POLITICO, Reuters headline).

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: Ukrainian and European sources may want to press Trump against territorial concessions, and U.S. sources may want to downplay conflict; neither side's incentive is proven.

target_audience.text: European and Ukrainian policymakers and publics, and readers tracking whether Trump will press Kyiv to cede Donbas.

confidence.reason: POLITICO was opened and presents both the FT account and a rebuttal. The FT and Reuters originals were not opened (FT paywalled, Reuters HTTP 401).

psyops.summary: Reports of a tense 10/17 meeting rested on anonymous sources who disagreed on details such as map-tossing, while agreeing Trump pushed toward ending the war on the current line and no Tomahawk commitment was made. The score applies to the contested account, not to POLITICO's careful reporting of it.
psyops.counter_argument: The substance (no Tomahawk promise, pressure on Donbas, 'current line') was reported consistently, and an EU diplomat called it 'not as bleak as reported', so the score is for color and sourcing, not the main outcome. Anonymity is normal in diplomatic reporting.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented): per BBC on 10/22, Trump shelved the planned Budapest meeting with Putin indefinitely and the U.S. sanctioned Rosneft and Lukoil. Trump said 'Every time I speak to Vladimir, I have good conversations and then they don't go anywhere'. That later shift was not knowable on 10/19.
gaps: The FT original (paywalled) and Reuters original (HTTP 401) were not opened.
All sourcing is anonymous, so no claim can be traced to a primary record.
The White House and Ukrainian presidential readouts were not opened.

psyops.headline: Trump terminates Canada trade talks again after Ontario runs ad featuring Reagan
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's 10/23 Truth Social claim that 'The Ronald Reagan Foundation has just announced that Canada has fraudulently used an advertisement, which is FAKE', and that Ontario ran it to interfere with the Supreme Court tariff case.
psyops.selection_reason: The claim attributes a stronger charge to a named foundation than its statement made, and a primary transcript and fact-checks exist.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: Trump cited the Reagan Foundation. Its statement said the ad 'misrepresents the Presidential Radio Address' and used 'selective audio and video', and that it was 'reviewing its legal options'. It did not say 'fake' or 'fraudulently' (NBC, PolitiFact). The claim that Ontario meant to interfere with the Supreme Court is unsupported in the sources read.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: The audio is Reagan's real 1987 address (Reagan Library transcript). PolitiFact/Poynter found the ad 'doesn't misrepresent Reagan's views on tariffs' overall, though it reordered sentences and left out his Japan-semiconductor exception.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'FAKE' and 'fraudulently' are stronger than a statement about editing, and are written in capitals.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Trump left out that the audio is genuine and that the Foundation's complaint was about selective editing and lack of permission. The White House later said the Foundation was 'calling out Ontario's misleading and selective editing' (PolitiFact).

emotional.label: documented

psyops.headline: Fact Check: Can Argentine Beef Really Lower U.S. Prices?
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's 10/19 statement aboard Air Force One, 'We would buy some beef from Argentina. If we do that, that will bring our beef prices down.'
psyops.selection_reason: Specific quantitative claim that can be tested against USDA import data.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The quote is on the record, from Trump, relayed by AP and quoted by DTN.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: DTN: Argentina is 'just under 2.2%' of U.S. beef and veal imports (98.9 million lb in 2024, USDA ERS), and the U.S. 'would have to become the largest buyer of Argentine beef to put a dent in beef prices'.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'That will bring our beef prices down' states a certain result.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Left out: imports are already at a record, Argentina is the eighth-largest exporter to the U.S., and about 75% of its exports go to China (DTN). The Reuters headline says the plan angered U.S. farmers; I did not read it.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: No fear or outrage hook.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: DTN says Trump 'has suggested' the same thing since the prior week, so the line was repeated.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: The administration gains if the $20 billion Argentina aid and the beef plan look beneficial to U.S. consumers, at a time of high beef prices (PolitiFact on the aid; DTN).

target_audience.text: U.S. consumers worried about beef prices, and critics of the Argentina swap facility among farmers and ranchers.

confidence.reason: DTN data and AP's quote were read; USDA ERS and Reuters/AP originals were not opened (Reuters HTTP 401, AP HTTP 403).

psyops.summary: Trump said buying Argentine beef would bring U.S. beef prices down. DTN's check found Argentina supplies about 2.2% of imports, so a dent in prices would require the U.S. to become Argentina's largest buyer. The score applies to the price claim, not to DTN's reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Added supply at the margin can reduce prices somewhat, and Trump may have meant a modest effect (inference). Argentina's beef exports to the U.S. rose nearly 46% in 2024 (DTN).
gaps: USDA ERS data were read only as quoted by DTN.
AP and Reuters originals were not opened (HTTP 403 and 401).
The claim was made on 10/19 (week 42, Sunday); the fact-check ran 10/20, so I placed it in week 43.

psyops.headline: Democrats and Republicans Clash Over SNAP Contingency Funds
psyops.scored_claim: USDA's website message (posted 10/25) and Speaker Johnson's 10/27 statement that SNAP funding 'has run dry', that 'there will be no benefits issued November 01', and that Democrats blocked the appropriation needed to use the contingency fund.
psyops.selection_reason: Official claim contradicted by the same agency's own earlier document, with a fact-check in the window.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The USDA message is unsigned. USDA's earlier position on the contingency fund was in its 9/30 'Lapse of Funding Plan', which has since been removed from USDA's site (FactCheck.org).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: FactCheck.org: 'We can't say whether the USDA is barred from tapping the contingency funds'; that may be a court decision. But the 9/30 plan said the multi-year contingency funds 'are also available to fund participant benefits in the event that a lapse occurs in the middle of the fiscal year', and the fund held about $5-6 billion.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'The well has run dry', 'gender mutilation procedures', 'healthcare for illegal aliens' (NBC, FactCheck.org).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The message leaves out the contingency reserve and USDA's earlier plan to use it. The '12 votes' were votes on Republican funding bills that lacked Democrats' health-care demands (FactCheck.org). The 'health care for illegal aliens' phrase was found misleading in earlier fact-checks (week 40 sources NBC, NPR, FactCheck.org).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: 'Mothers, babies, and the most vulnerable among us' is a fear hook placed on an official government page (NBC).

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: The White House spokesperson, USDA and Johnson used the same 'Democrats' shutdown' line within days (NBC, FactCheck.org). The messaging coordination beyond ordinary party discipline was not shown.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: The source is the administration, which controls the funds and gains if the public blames Democrats. Democrats say the administration chose not to continue payments as leverage (FactCheck.org).

target_audience.text: SNAP recipients and the general public, steered to blame Senate Democrats for the shutdown; secondary audience is Senate Democrats being pressured on the funding vote.

confidence.reason: I read FactCheck.org and NBC in full, and NPR's account of the 10/27 lawsuit. I did not retrieve the 9/30 plan (removed from USDA's site; FactCheck.org says it is on the Wayback Machine).

psyops.mechanism: Documented: USDA's own 9/30 plan described the contingency fund as available for benefits in a mid-year lapse, then USDA's website told the public that 'the well has run dry' and framed the lapse as Democrats' choice. The plan was removed from USDA's site.
psyops.summary: On 10/25 USDA posted a banner saying SNAP benefits would stop 11/1 and blaming Senate Democrats. FactCheck.org found the agency's position had changed from its own 9/30 plan, and that the question of whether the contingency fund can be used is a legal one. Reporting by NBC, NPR and FactCheck.org was accurate; the score applies to the claim.
psyops.counter_argument: The administration's legal argument is that the contingency fund needs a prior appropriation, and FactCheck.org says the question may be for the courts. Past USDA plans (2019, 2021) did assume contingency funds would pay benefits, but they were written under different circumstances. Democrats did vote against the Republican stopgap 12 times. Both sides used the shutdown for leverage.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented, not knowable on 10/31): on 11/6 Judge McConnell (D.R.I., Doc. 34) found the administration's stated reasons 'pretextual' and that SNAP benefits were being withheld for political reasons. The order notes the 'well has run dry' language had disappeared from USDA's website and that USDA acknowledged in 2019 that contingency funds could fund SNAP in a shutdown. The ruling is preliminary and was appealed.
gaps: The 9/30 USDA Lapse of Funding Plan was not opened; quoted from FactCheck.org.
The Newsweek fact-check returned HTTP 406 to automated access and was not read.
The USDA banner was read through NBC and FactCheck.org; I did not view the live page, which has since changed.
The banner was posted 10/25 (week 43). The week-44 items are Johnson's 10/27 statement and the 10/31 fact-check.

psyops.headline: US kills 14 in strikes on four alleged drug boats in Pacific
psyops.scored_claim: Hegseth's 10/27-28 statement that the four vessels were 'known by our intelligence apparatus, transitioning along known narco-trafficking routes and carrying narcotics' and that those killed were 'narco-terrorists'.
psyops.selection_reason: Official claim attached to a lethal action, with no public evidence, and an independent fact-check on 10/30.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: FactCheck.org: Hegseth 'did not provide the identities of the people on the boats, evidence of what drugs they were transporting, or other details.' The same is true of earlier strikes.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Nothing public identifies cargo, cartel affiliation or occupants. Colombia's president said one earlier strike killed a fisherman. Rand Paul said 'No one said their name. No one said what evidence' (FactCheck.org).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Narco-terrorists', 'hunt and kill', and comparison to al Qaeda (FactCheck.org, BBC).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Left out: the administration's 'armed conflict' legal theory was given to Congress in a confidential notice, and experts question it (FactCheck.org, BBC). FactCheck.org notes Trump's 10/18 'mostly Fentanyl' claim sits oddly with Venezuela and Colombia's roles.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Videos of boats being destroyed are posted with each announcement (BBC).

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: The phrase 'known narco-trafficking routes' recurs in Hegseth's posts across strikes (FactCheck.org); the repetition is documented but not necessarily coordination.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: The administration is the sole source and needs the 'terrorist' label to support the legal basis for continuing the strikes.

target_audience.text: U.S. public and Congress, to sustain support for a lethal campaign and a possible expansion to land targets; secondary audience is Venezuela, Colombia and Mexico.

confidence.reason: BBC and FactCheck.org agree on what was and was not shown. I did not open Hegseth's post, the CNN article or Reuters/AP originals directly. The facts of the strikes themselves are confirmed by Mexico's search for a survivor (BBC).

psyops.mechanism: Documented: each strike is announced with the same 'narco-terrorist', 'known routes' wording and a video, but no identities, cargo evidence or occupants' affiliations are released, while the administration told Congress the U.S. is in an 'armed conflict' with cartels.
psyops.summary: On 10/27 U.S. forces struck boats in the eastern Pacific, killing 14 and leaving one survivor. The administration said the boats carried narcotics and the dead were 'narco-terrorists', but showed no evidence of cargo or identity. The strikes happened; the score applies to the unevidenced characterization, not to outlets' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Some of these boats may well carry cocaine: the Times reported boats from Venezuela and Colombia do smuggle it, and the administration says classified intelligence supports the labels (FactCheck.org, BBC). Survivors from an earlier strike were repatriated, not tried, which the administration says reflects its handling. Expert and congressional criticism is bipartisan (BBC).
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window: not checked. FactCheck.org's page was updated 12/22/2025, so I used only its text about events through 10/28.
gaps: Hegseth's X post and the videos were not opened.

CNN's page is very large; only BBC and FactCheck.org text was used.
The classified intelligence cannot be examined.

psyops.headline: Trump directs nuclear weapons testing to resume for first time in over 30 years
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's 10/29 Truth Social post: 'Because of other countries testing programs, I have instructed the Department of War to start testing our Nuclear Weapons on an equal basis.'
psyops.selection_reason: A short, high-stakes announcement whose stated premise (others are testing) can be checked.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: A single post, with no program or country named. The text is on trumpstruth.org (archive of the post). Trump later said test sites would be determined later (BBC).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: The Kremlin said its Burevestnik and Poseidon tests were 'not nuclear' and 'cannot in any way be interpreted as a nuclear test'. BBC and the Arms Control Association say no country except North Korea has conducted a nuclear explosive test this century. Trump's 'more Nuclear Weapons than any other country' is also contradicted by the FAS counts BBC cites (Russia about 5,459, U.S. about 5,177).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Equal basis' and 'start immediately' sound decisive but are vague about what will be tested.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The post did not say whether it meant explosive tests or delivery-system tests; BBC says the White House issued no clarification.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Mentions of Russia and China and a 'distant third' fall short of fear-based language, but the timing, minutes before the Xi meeting, raises the stakes (BBC).

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: No coordinated push seen beyond normal coverage.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: The announcement came as Trump met Xi and about 100 days before New START expires (BBC); it may be leverage in arms talks (inference).

target_audience.text: Russia and China (a signal ahead of the Xi meeting and New START expiry), and a domestic audience favoring a strong-defense image.

confidence.reason: I read the BBC articles and the archived post text. The Reuters and AP originals were not opened (HTTP 401/403).

psyops.summary: Trump announced the U.S. would start testing nuclear weapons 'on an equal basis' because of other countries' testing programs. Russia's recent tests were of delivery systems, and the Kremlin denied any nuclear test. It was unclear whether Trump meant explosive tests. The score applies to the premise and the ambiguity, not to outlets' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Russia and China do run programs that carry nuclear weapons (Burevestnik and Poseidon are nuclear-powered or nuclear-capable), and non-explosive 'testing' of the U.S. arsenal is routine (BBC). The post may have meant systems tests.
psyops.hindsight_note: Within the week (11/2, documented): per an AP headline in search results that I did not open, Energy Secretary Wright said the tests would not include nuclear explosions. This was headline-level only, and I could not open AP (403).
gaps: The Truth Social post itself was read through trumpstruth.org, not truthsocial.com.

psyops.headline: Are Christians being persecuted in Nigeria as Trump claims?
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's 10/31 Truth Social post: 'Christianity is facing an existential threat in Nigeria. Thousands of Christians are being killed. Radical Islamists are responsible for this mass slaughter', citing '3,100 versus 4,476 Worldwide'.
psyops.selection_reason: Quantitative claim used to justify a country designation and a threat of military action, with in-window BBC verification work.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The post cites numbers but not a source; a White House official told the BBC the 3,100 figure comes from an Open Doors report on the 12 months from October 2023 (BBC).

verifiability.label: disputed
verifiability.note: BBC: some of the data behind these claims is 'difficult to verify'. Open Doors' own data records 3,100 Christians and 2,320 Muslims killed in that period. Other monitors say the number of Christians killed is far lower and most victims of jihadist groups are Muslims (BBC).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Existential threat' and 'mass slaughter' go beyond what the underlying data says about motive; Nigeria's government called the framing 'a gross misrepresentation of reality' (BBC).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The post leaves out that the same Open Doors report counts 2,320 Muslim deaths in the period, and that Open Doors says Fulani militant groups were responsible for a third of Christian deaths in the Middle Belt (BBC, corrected 11/10).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Religious-persecution framing ('slaughtered') is a strong identity hook for Trump's Christian base.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Similar numbers circulated through Sen. Cruz (10/7), Bill Maher, and Rep. Riley Moore, traced largely to one NGO, InterSociety (BBC). The BBC could not match that NGO's totals to its cited reports.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: Trump gains domestic support from a Christian-defence frame and a pretext for action; the source of the figure (Open Doors) is an advocacy charity (BBC).

target_audience.text: Evangelical and Christian U.S. voters and Congress members; secondarily the Nigerian government, pressed with a threat of sanctions or force.

confidence.reason: I read the BBC analysis and Trump's post text (American Presidency Project) and The Conversation's ACLED analysis. I did not open ACLED data, Open Doors' report or the AP piece (HTTP 403).

psyops.summary: Trump said thousands of Christians are being killed in Nigeria by radical Islamists. Violence there is real and deadly, but the BBC found the data behind the 'Christian genocide' framing is hard to verify and that Muslims are also killed in large numbers, including in the same Open Doors report Trump's figure came from. The score applies to the framing and omission, not to the BBC's reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Attacks on Christians in Nigeria are real, and Open Doors recorded 3,100 Christian deaths that year; USCIRF recommended the 'country of particular concern' label (The Conversation). Christians are sometimes targeted, according to Open Doors' researcher quoted by the BBC.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window: not checked. The BBC page was updated after 11/5 (a 11/10 correction and later paragraphs); I used only its data analysis.

psyops.headline: Experts Raise Doubts About Trump's Dividend Payment Proposal
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's 11/9 Truth Social claim: 'We are taking in Trillions of Dollars [from tariffs]... A dividend of at least $2000 a person (not including high income people!) will be paid to everyone.'
psyops.selection_reason: Numeric claim with public Treasury data to test it and a concrete promise with no plan behind it.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The post is on the record (American Presidency Project). No plan or source for 'trillions' was given and the White House did not answer FactCheck.org.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: FactCheck.org: the U.S. 'has not made trillions of dollars' from tariffs; Trump appears to count pledged private investments. Treasury data cited by FactCheck.org show about $195 billion in customs duties in fiscal 2025. No formal plan was approved by Congress and no checks were scheduled.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'People that are against Tariffs are FOOLS!' is loaded, and 'will be paid to everyone' states a certainty.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Left out: cost near $300 billion per round (Tax Foundation, via FactCheck.org); the Supreme Court case that could erase much tariff revenue (PolitiFact); and that importers, not foreign countries, mostly pay the tariffs (Tax Policy Center, via FactCheck.org).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: No fear or outrage hook; a payment promise.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Trump repeated the pitch on 11/10 in the Oval Office and in a second post (FactCheck.org, PolitiFact).

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: Trump gains politically from a popular payment promise while the Supreme Court weighs the tariffs, and a bogus 'direct deposit' hoax spread on top of it (FactCheck.org).

target_audience.text: Voters worried about costs, and the Supreme Court and tariff critics (the post is aimed at defending tariffs).

confidence.reason: I read the post text at the American Presidency Project and read FactCheck.org and PolitiFact. The Treasury and Tax Foundation figures are quoted from them. The fact-checks were published 11/10 and 11/14, after the week.

psyops.summary: On 11/9 Trump said tariffs bring in 'trillions' and promised a $2,000 dividend. Fact-checkers found tariff revenue far below trillions and no plan or funding for the payment. The promise is a proposal, not a scheduled payment. The score applies to the claim, not to the fact-checkers' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Tariff collections did rise sharply (PolitiFact: $309.2 billion through October versus $165.4 billion the year before), and Trump described the dividend as a plan, not a delivered payment. The Tax Policy Center and CRFB figures show the idea is arithmetic-limited, not impossible.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented): FactCheck.org (updated 11/14) and PolitiFact (11/10) rated the claims. The revenue figures they use were public before 11/9.
gaps: The claim was made on Sunday 11/9, the last day of the week; both fact-checks fall in week 46.
Treasury and Tax Foundation sources were read only through FactCheck.org and PolitiFact.
The FactCheck.org page was updated on 11/14; I did not separate its later edits from its original text.
Dating flag: the primary url is dated 11/14/2025, outside this week's window (11/03/2025 to 11/09/2025). Dates were not altered; check the placement before relying on it.

psyops.headline: BBC apologises to Trump over edited speech but rejects compensation claim
psyops.scored_claim: The Panorama clip (aired a week before the 2024 U.S. election) that spliced Trump's 1/6/2021 speech to suggest he said: 'We're going to walk down to the Capitol and I'll be there with you, and we fight. We fight like hell.'
psyops.selection_reason: A broadcaster conceded its own edit was misleading; a primary transcript exists to test it.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The clip used Trump's real words from a real speech, but spliced sections 'almost an hour apart' (Guardian).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: The NPR transcript has 'we're going to walk down' near the end and 'fight like hell' earlier; Trump also said supporters would march to the Capitol 'to peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard'. The BBC's chair said the edit gave the impression 'of a direct call for violent action'.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: The spliced clip made separate passages sound like one command; the BBC apologised for 'the manner in which the video clip was edited'.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The 'peacefully and patriotically' passage was left out, and the 'fight like hell' passage came earlier without reference to the Capitol (NPR transcript).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: The scene is built around a 1/6 call to violence, a high-emotion subject for the audience.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: I found no sign of a coordinated push; the programme aired once and the concern surfaced a year later in a memo (Guardian).

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive not shown
incentive.note: The BBC says the splice was unintentional and there is no evidence of a motive in the reporting. Per the Guardian, a memo by former BBC adviser Michael Prescott raised concerns about the edit and alleged systemic bias, which the BBC denies.

target_audience.text: British and international viewers of the BBC documentary in the week before the U.S. election.

confidence.reason: I read the Guardian's report of the BBC's statement, the transcript of the speech (NPR), and found the BBC's own admission of the edit. I did not watch the program. The BBC disputes the memo's claim of systemic bias and the defamation claim.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: a clip joined sections of Trump's speech almost an hour apart and omitted his call to march 'peacefully and patriotically', and the BBC apologised for the edit. Intent is not shown, and the BBC says it was unintentional.
psyops.summary: A Panorama episode spliced two parts of Trump's 1/6/2021 speech into one sentence. The BBC chair apologised on 11/13 and the programme will not be rebroadcast; the BBC rejects Trump's defamation claim and $1 billion demand. Intent is not shown.
psyops.counter_argument: Some in the BBC argue the edit did not change the meaning of the speech significantly (Guardian). Trump's speech did include 'fight like hell' and 'walk down' lines, and the BBC rejects the claim that the edit defamed him.
psyops.hindsight_note: This entry scores the coverage as it ran in 2024 (a week before the election) and reports 2025 events, so the 11/13 apology is a later documented outcome rather than something knowable then.

The Telegraph's memo story and the AP report were not opened (AP blocked, HTTP 403 for AP generally).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: CNN cites CPI data: coffee cost nearly 20% more in September than a year earlier, with 50% tariffs on Brazil, the top supplier; tomato prices rose after the 17% Mexico tariff. The White House's own rollback undercuts the claim.

emotional.label: documented

amplification.label: documented

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference

target_audience.text: U.S. consumers worried about grocery prices and swing voters after the 11/4 elections.

confidence.reason: I read NPR and CNN, which agree. I did not open the executive order or Reuters (HTTP 401).

psyops.headline: Donald Trump said Democrats' call to military amounts to sedition. Experts say that's doubtful
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's 11/20 Truth Social posts that six Democratic lawmakers' video telling service members they can 'refuse illegal orders' was 'SEDITIOUS BEHAVIOR AT THE HIGHEST LEVEL' by 'traitors' who should be 'ARRESTED AND PUT ON TRIAL'.
psyops.selection_reason: A legal-sounding accusation checkable against the video text and legal experts, with a documented later outcome.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The posts are on the record and quoted by PolitiFact and FactCheck.org; the video text is quoted in full by PolitiFact.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Legal experts told PolitiFact they see 'no path' to charge the lawmakers under any sedition law: 'They are not conspiring to overthrow the government,' said Rod Smolla. FactCheck.org's experts agree. Federal seditious conspiracy carries up to 20 years, not death (search excerpt of PolitiFact/FactCheck.org).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'TRAITORS', 'LOCK THEM UP???', 'ARRESTED AND PUT ON TRIAL', 'An example MUST BE SET' (PolitiFact).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The posts leave out that the video said 'You can refuse illegal orders' and did not name any orders, and that the law bars carrying out unlawful orders. The White House said the video could 'inspire chaos' by encouraging disobedience of 'lawful' orders (PolitiFact).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Fear and tribal hooks: 'We won't have a Country anymore!!!' (PolitiFact).

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Hegseth ('Stage 4 Trump Derangement Syndrome') and Sen. Blackburn echoed the condemnation the same day, which is ordinary party messaging (PolitiFact).

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: The president attacks critics who say an administration directive might be illegal, as he is the one giving orders; Slotkin tied her concerns to the Caribbean boat strikes (PolitiFact).

target_audience.text: Trump's supporters, the military audience the video addressed, and Democratic lawmakers who are chilled from speaking.

confidence.reason: I read PolitiFact's text with the video transcript and Trump's quoted posts. I could not open Reuters (HTTP 401) or AP (HTTP 403); the 'punishable by DEATH' wording is from their headlines and I did not see the post text itself.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: Trump labelled a restatement of military law as 'sedition' and demanded arrest, while legal experts found no legal basis for any sedition charge. The later outcome (below) was a grand jury declining to indict.
psyops.summary: After a video in which six Democratic lawmakers told service members they can and must refuse illegal orders, Trump called it sedition by traitors who should be arrested. Legal experts said it was not sedition. The White House said Trump did not want to execute lawmakers. The score applies to Trump's characterization, not to the outlets' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Service members must obey lawful orders, and some Republicans said public calls to disobey could disrupt the chain of command (PolitiFact). The video did not name orders, so critics said it was vague. The White House said Trump did not seek to execute members of Congress.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented, not knowable on 11/20): per CNN (2/12/2026), a D.C. grand jury declined to approve charges against Sen. Kelly and other lawmakers, and Judge Richard Leon ruled Hegseth's action against Kelly was unconstitutional retaliation.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Wicker and Reed (a Republican and a Democrat) announced an investigation after the report (Guardian); coverage then spread widely.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The fraud involved specific federal cases (Feeding Our Future, Medicaid housing and autism programs) charged against individuals (FactCheck.org).

amplification.note: The reported ICE operation in the Twin Cities was planned at the same time (BBC, citing CBS), and the White House defended the remarks (FactCheck.org); I found no sign of a coordinated message campaign.

incentive.note: The administration is the source; BBC notes Trump attacked Rep. Ilhan Omar and Minnesota Democrats and was expanding an immigration crackdown. Motive is inference.

psyops.headline: Trump's pardon comments omit why former Honduran president Juan Orlando Hernández was prosecuted
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's 11/30–12/1 claim that Honduras' former president Hernández was 'set up' by the Biden administration, and the White House line (Leavitt, 12/1) that his case was 'over-prosecution' of someone 'opposed to the values of the previous administration'.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: A jury convicted Hernández after a three-week trial; Judge Castel sentenced him to 45 years in June 2024 and a new-trial motion was denied (PolitiFact, FactCheck.org, Al Jazeera).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Set up' and 'over-prosecution' recast a drug-trafficking conviction as political persecution.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: PolitiFact says the pardon comments omit why he was prosecuted: over 400 tons of cocaine, with testimony from former traffickers and bribes funding his political rise. Al Jazeera notes Trump praised his anti-drug work in 2019.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: The pardon was announced while the US was striking alleged 'narco-terrorists' (PolitiFact), a contrast that critics stressed.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Leavitt repeated the line at the 12/1 briefing (PolitiFact), but I found no wider coordination.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: Al Jazeera noted Trump-backed candidate Nasry Asfura led the Honduran vote count, but no source I read links that to the pardon; the motive is not established.

target_audience.text: Trump's base and Honduran and Latin American conservative allies; also Congress members who criticised the pardon (inference).

confidence.reason: I read PolitiFact, FactCheck.org and Al Jazeera, all consistent on the court record. I did not read the trial record or DOJ press release myself.

psyops.summary: Trump said Hernández was 'set up' by Biden and pardoned him. Three fact-checks found no evidence of a set-up and a jury conviction after a three-week trial. This scores the claim, not the fact-checks' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Trump argued a foreign president was singled out. PolitiFact notes that prosecuting a foreign leader is unusual but not unprecedented (Noriega, Lazarenko). The pardon power is Trump's by law, and Leavitt criticised the trial as scant on evidence.

psyops.headline: FactChecking Trump's Economic Speech
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's 12/9 Mount Pocono, Pennsylvania speech claims: 'inflation is stopped', gasoline at '$1.99 a gallon' in 'three or four states', credit for 4,000 new Pennsylvania manufacturing jobs, and 'more Americans are working today' than ever.
psyops.selection_reason: A campaign-style rally on affordability before the 2026 midterms, with checkable numbers.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: Trump said these on the record at a televised rally (FactCheck.org, PolitiFact).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: FactCheck.org: inflation was 3% for the 12 months ending in September, and Fed chair Powell said on 12/10 that inflation 'remains somewhat elevated'. The lowest state gas average was Oklahoma at $2.37; the national average was $2.94. U.S. manufacturing jobs were down 49,000 since January (BLS).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Inflation is stopped' is an absolute; PolitiFact says Trump has tried to paint affordability concerns as a 'hoax' and a Democratic issue.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The $1.99 claim omits that it applies to a few dozen stations, not any state average (GasBuddy via PolitiFact). The jobs claim omits the national drop in manufacturing jobs, and 'more Americans working' is largely population growth with a slightly lower employment-population ratio (FactCheck.org).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: The claims are about prices and jobs, not fear.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: FactCheck.org says Trump has made the same claims many times before; the repetition is documented.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: It was a campaign-style rally before the midterms (FactCheck.org, PolitiFact); motive is inference.

target_audience.text: Pennsylvania voters and swing-state voters worried about prices (inference).

confidence.reason: I read FactCheck.org (12/11) fully and PolitiFact (12/10) in part. Other claims in the speech, including the immigration remarks, are not scored here.

psyops.summary: In a Pennsylvania rally speech Trump said inflation had stopped, gas was $1.99 in several states and manufacturing was growing. Fact-checkers found CPI inflation at 3%, no state average near $1.99, and manufacturing jobs down 49,000. This scores the claims as stated, not the fact-checkers' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Some claims are true: oil prices have fallen about 25% since January (WTI $59.04 vs $78.56) and national gas is below $3. Some stations do charge $1.99 or less (GasBuddy). Both fact-checkers credit those points.

emotional.label: documented

amplification.label: documented

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference

psyops.scored_claim: The administration's framing of the 12/25 Nigeria strikes as a response to persecution of Christians (Trump has 'claimed a "genocide"', per BBC) and Trump's account to Politico that he ordered them as 'a Christmas present'.
psyops.selection_reason: A military strike framed as protecting Christians, contradicted in part by Nigeria and by outside data.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: Trump's Politico interview and earlier statements are quoted by BBC; I could not retrieve his Truth Social post, so the 'persecution' wording rests on BBC and NBC's description.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: AFRICOM confirmed strikes on ISIS in Sokoto with 'multiple' deaths. BBC: most victims of violence in Nigeria are Muslims, according to ACLED; a local official said 'there is no conflict between us and Christians'; Nigeria strongly denies systematic persecution (NBC).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: BBC says the Trump administration has 'claimed a "genocide"' against Christians; Nigeria's foreign minister said the operation had 'nothing to do with a particular religion'.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: BBC and NBC: Nigeria said it was a joint operation planned 'for quite some time' with Nigerian intelligence and the president's 'explicit approval'; Trump told Politico he chose the timing as 'a Christmas present'. The framing omits that most victims are Muslims (ACLED).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: The 'Christmas present' remark and 'powerful and deadly' language are emotive (BBC).

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: The story was carried by BBC, NBC, Reuters and AFRICOM within a day; the 'Christians' framing was pushed by the administration (BBC, NBC).

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is inference
incentive.note: NBC says Trump threatened action last month unless Nigeria stopped what he called persecution; the administration's domestic religious audience is inference.

target_audience.text: Trump's Christian conservative base and evangelical supporters at home, and Nigeria's government as the audience for pressure (inference).

confidence.reason: I read BBC and NBC (12/26) and AFRICOM's release. I could not retrieve Trump's post, and Reuters' reports were not opened (401).

psyops.summary: The US struck ISIS-linked camps in Nigeria. Trump framed it around persecution of Christians. Nigeria said it was a joint counter-terrorism operation with 'nothing to do with a particular religion', and ACLED data say most victims are Muslims. This scores the framing, not BBC's reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: AFRICOM and Nigerian officials agree militants were killed. Nigeria cooperated, so the strike was not unilateral (NBC). Some Nigerian Christians do face violence; BBC notes the persecution question is contested, and a framing of 'a joint operation' does not exclude a protective motive.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window: none read; a Reuters report on 12/27 that Nigeria said two camps were hit was not opened (401).

psyops.headline: Trump says US will 'run' Venezuela and claims Venezuela 'stole' American oil after capturing Maduro
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's justification that Venezuela 'unilaterally seized and stole American oil, American assets and American platforms' and that the US will 'run' Venezuela and get 'total access' to its oil (not the capture itself, which is documented).

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The claim comes from Trump's own statements (press conference, Air Force One), with no document offered. The underlying history is real: Venezuela nationalised foreign oil operations in 1976, and ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips later won arbitration awards (ABC Australia, read in the search excerpt).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: ABC quotes economist Francisco Rodríguez calling the 'stole' claim 'false, completely'. The Guardian quotes legal scholar José Ignacio Hernández: 'Venezuela did not steal any oil from the US', and other analysts note US firms held concessions, not ownership.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Stole' and 'run' are loaded terms for a contested compensation dispute. Experts quoted by SBS call foreign control of the resource potentially a 'hostile occupation'. Rubio told NBC the same day that 'there's not a war' with Venezuela, only against drug trafficking organizations.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The claim leaves out that US companies were compensated roughly US$1 billion in the 1970s and that the later awards were being paid until sanctions halted Venezuelan oil sales (ABC Australia). The 'stole' wording is partial context, not an invented fact.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Grievance hook ('stole American oil') paired with a promise of money for the country. It is not the main content of the reporting.

amplification.label: disputed
amplification.note: The oil theme was repeated across Trump's appearances. The Guardian argues the focus 'reinforces claim action was never about war on drugs'. That reading is an interpretation and the administration says the aim is stopping drug trafficking (Rubio, NBC).

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The speaker is the party that gains legal and political cover for the operation and for US oil access. Whether that was the purpose is inference.

target_audience.text: US domestic audiences asked to support an unauthorised military operation, and the oil industry and investors; Venezuelan exiles are a secondary audience.

confidence.reason: I read Reuters, NBC and search excerpts of ABC Australia, the Guardian, SBS and ICLG. The legal expert quotes agree with each other, but they are commentary, and I could not open the Trump transcript directly.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: the operation was described as a law-enforcement action on drug charges, while the post-operation messaging added a theft-of-oil grievance that experts quoted by the Guardian and ABC say has no legal basis.
psyops.summary: Trump announced on Jan 3 that US forces had captured Nicolás Maduro and his wife and that the US would 'run' Venezuela until a transition and use US oil companies to fix the oil industry. Within a day he and aides added the claim that Venezuela had stolen US oil assets. Reuters, AP and NBC reported the operation accurately. The score applies to the 'stole' and 'run' framing, not to the reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: The 1976 nationalisation and the unpaid arbitration awards are real grievances, and a legal claim to compensation exists, as ABC notes. Trump's allies can fairly say his phrase compresses a genuine dispute.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: He conceded that 'the bazaaris were right' about the economic conditions (Reuters), so the grievance was not hidden, but he omitted state economic policy as a cause, blaming 'the enemy' for the rial's fall (AP).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Religious and national-identity hooks ('chanting slogans against Islam, Iran'), plus the threat of force, but the speech also contains concrete economic acknowledgement.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: AP notes the foreign-instigation claim is one 'constantly made by officials', so it follows a standard pattern. It came a day after Trump's warning that the US 'will come to their rescue' (AP, Euronews), which the regime uses as supporting context.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The speaker is the government that would face the consequences of the protests, and gains from delegitimising them. Motive is an inference.

psyops.headline: Videos contradict Trump's and Noem's account of fatal ICE shooting of Renee Good in Minneapolis
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's post that the driver 'violently, willfully, and viciously ran over the ICE Officer' and Noem's label of 'an act of domestic terrorism', issued within hours of the Jan 7 shooting.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The account came from the President and DHS Secretary within hours, before any investigation, with no evidence cited. The FBI investigation was still open (NBC).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: NBC's video review: Good's car 'did not knock down the officer, whose legs were to the side of the SUV'; the officer walked away unassisted. PolitiFact reports New York Times and Washington Post frame-by-frame analyses found the agent stepped aside and fired at least two of three shots from the side.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Viciously ran over', 'violent rioter' and 'domestic terrorism' are loaded words. PolitiFact experts say the label has no legal basis here; Michael German: 'entirely pejorative and prejudicial'.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Omitted that, per NBC's video, her wheels were turned right, away from the officers, when the first shot was fired, and that she was a US citizen with no criminal background who had just dropped her son at school (PolitiFact, citing AP).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Fear and tribal hooks: 'domestic terrorist', 'violent rioter', 'It is hard to believe he is alive' (Trump, quoted by NBC), while the officer walked away.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Trump, Noem and DHS used the same self-defence and terrorism framing at once. PolitiFact notes DHS used a similar 'domestic terrorist' description in the October Chicago shooting of Marimar Martinez, whose federal charges were later dismissed. It is a repeated pattern, not proof of coordination.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The accounts came from the agency whose officer fired, which gains from a self-defence finding. Motive is an inference.

target_audience.text: Supporters of the administration's immigration enforcement and the public during a live investigation; critics and Minnesota officials are the opponents the framing targets.

confidence.reason: I read NBC's video analysis and PolitiFact via PBS directly; the Washington Post and AP pieces were seen as search excerpts. The video evidence is public. The FBI investigation was ongoing and the full record was not public.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: officials publicly characterised the victim as a domestic terrorist within hours, and videos reviewed by NBC, the Times and the Post show a different sequence than the one officials described.
psyops.summary: On Jan 7 an ICE officer shot and killed Renee Nicole Good in Minneapolis. Trump said she 'viciously ran over' the officer and Noem called it domestic terrorism. NBC and others analysed videos that show her vehicle turning away as the officer fired. The score applies to the official characterisation, not to the outlets' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Videos show the SUV moving toward the officer and the officer fired from near the vehicle, so a fear for his safety is not absurd (Washington Post, via search). Stanford's Shirin Sinnar says intentional ramming could be terrorism in another context, and the investigation was not finished.
psyops.hindsight_note: Hindsight (documented, after the window; not knowable at the time): As of an Oct 1, 2026 search excerpt, Officer Jonathan Ross had not been charged, Hennepin County's investigation remained open, and DOJ declined to open a criminal civil-rights probe, saying it saw no basis (AP via search; I could not open the full pages). These later facts do not settle what was knowable on Jan 8-10, when the videos already contradicted the claim.

psyops.headline: EPA and Trump say repealing the endangerment finding 'will save American taxpayers over $1.3 trillion' and $2,400 per vehicle
psyops.scored_claim: Zeldin's and Trump's Feb 12 claim that the repeal 'will save American taxpayers over $1.3 trillion' and 'over $2,400 for a new vehicle', repeated in EPA fact sheets and by Trump, Vought and Leavitt.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The figures come from EPA's own regulatory impact analysis, a real primary document. FactCheck.org traces $1.1 trillion avoided vehicle-technology costs plus $200 billion avoided EV charger costs for 2027-2055.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: The $1.3 trillion 'is not a net total' (FactCheck.org). In EPA's own central scenario using EIA fuel prices, repeal costs Americans $180 billion net, even before health or climate effects.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Save... over $1.3 trillion' and 'single largest deregulatory action in U.S. history' (EPA release headline) present gross avoided cost as savings. NYU's Jason Schwartz: 'a very biased and misleading way to talk about the effects'.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Omits higher fuel and maintenance costs, and EPA 'is no longer monetizing benefits' from reduced pollution; EDF estimated up to 58,000 more premature deaths through 2055 (FactCheck.org). The $2,400 figure is not a price cut: it is avoided cost, not lower sticker price (Gillingham).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Appeals to 'lower prices, more choices', and 'heavy-handed climate policies' are mild affordability hooks.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: The same figure was repeated by Zeldin, Trump, Vought, Leavitt and EPA communications; FactCheck.org notes Yale's Kenneth Gillingham 'can't recall another rulemaking where' fact sheets focused only on costs.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The source is the agency issuing the rule and the administration that wants to justify it; it chose which scenarios to emphasise (only two of four 3% scenarios exceed $1.3 trillion).

target_audience.text: Car buyers and households worried about prices, plus the courts and the public that will judge the repeal's justification; automakers and the fossil-fuel industry benefit.

confidence.reason: I read the FactCheck.org analysis in full; the EPA release returned HTTP 200 but I read its content only through the search summary and FactCheck.org's quotes. Bloomberg and AP were seen as excerpts. The analysis includes an expert Science critique published later.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: a gross avoided-cost figure from a regulatory analysis was publicised as 'savings' while the same analysis's central scenario shows a net cost, and health benefits were set at zero.
psyops.summary: On Feb 12 EPA rescinded the 2009 endangerment finding and the vehicle emissions standards, and officials said it saves $1.3 trillion and $2,400 per vehicle. FactCheck.org, Bloomberg and AP analysts later said the number counts only costs avoided, not the costs of repeal. The score applies to the savings claim, not to the legal action itself.
psyops.counter_argument: EPA says it presented eight net impacts across scenarios and 'didn't single out scenarios to suit a narrative'. Most of its modelled scenarios do show net savings if health and climate benefits are excluded, and EPA argues the effect on non-GHG pollutants is 'marginal'.
psyops.hindsight_note: Hindsight (documented, after the window; not knowable at the time): FactCheck.org's Sept 3 update reports a Science paper (Aug 27) by Gillingham, Jacobsen and colleagues finding EPA overestimated savings by about $540 billion and underestimated costs by $920 billion, implying a $670 billion net cost rather than EPA's $790 billion net savings. Bloomberg (Feb 19) reported the EPA's math differed from the $1.3 trillion headline. None of this was in public view on Feb 12.
gaps: The fact-check is dated March 17 (updated Sept 3), outside the window; the claim and the EPA release are Feb 12 (in window).
The EPA's regulatory impact analysis itself was not opened; its numbers are as quoted by FactCheck.org.
