psyops.headline: Musk and Trump amplify a long-debunked claim that Pennsylvania 'received back around 2.5 million' mail ballots after sending 1.8 million
psyops.scored_claim: A Feb 8 X post, reposted by Elon Musk ('Essential to stop fraud in elections') and by Trump on Feb 10, that in 2020 'Pennsylvania sent out 1,823,148 mail-in ballots but received back around 2.5 MILLION', accounting for a 'fraudulent' Biden vote spike.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The claim traces to a Nov 25, 2020 Pennsylvania Senate GOP hearing where Rudy Giuliani cited the figures; a witness, Phil Waldron, speculated about machine tampering and later invoked the Fifth Amendment before the Jan 6 committee (FactCheck.org). The poster is an X account, The SCIF.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Pennsylvania's Department of State report shows 2,673,272 mail-in ballot applications approved for the 2020 general election and 2,273,490 mail votes cast. MIT's Charles Stewart: the claim 'is based on mixing up statistics from the primary and the general election'.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Steal the 2020 election', 'fraudulent and impossible' and 'Trump won in a landslide' are loaded; the post also claims Pennsylvania's Secretary of State 'wiped' a number, which FactCheck.org does not corroborate.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Compares the 2020 primary send-out (~1.8 million) to the general-election returns (~2.5 million), a mismatch of two elections, and omits the publicly available data (FactCheck.org).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: An election-theft accusation hook, but the post is data-based in form.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Musk reposted twice and Trump reposted the claim on Feb 10 without comment, while Congress considers the SAVE America Act (FactCheck.org); Stewart: 'long-ago debunked claims that will not disappear despite the availability of official data'.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The amplifiers are political actors who want mail voting curtailed and the claim supports that policy; their sincerity is not something I can establish.

target_audience.text: Trump's and Musk's followers, and members of Congress weighing election-rule legislation such as the SAVE America Act.

confidence.reason: I read the FactCheck.org piece in full. It links the Pennsylvania state report, which I did not open, and quotes an MIT expert and a former Pennsylvania election official.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: a statistic from the 2020 primary was compared with 2020 general-election counts to suggest 700,000 phantom ballots, and the error was recirculated by high-reach accounts.
psyops.summary: On Feb 8-10 the Pennsylvania ballot claim, first aired in 2020, was reposted by Musk and Trump to support abolishing most mail voting. FactCheck.org (Feb 13) showed the numbers mix two different elections. The score applies to the claim and its amplification, not to FactCheck.org.
psyops.counter_argument: Mail-in voting policy is a legitimate dispute; Musk and Trump can argue for limits without this statistic. Some people have raised sincere security concerns about mail ballots, though that does not support the Pennsylvania number.
psyops.hindsight_note: Hindsight (documented, after the window; not knowable at the time): I did not search for later developments on the SAVE America Act or the claim in this scan.

psyops.headline: Doctored CBC video and Telegram posts claim Ukrainian athletes at the Milano Cortina Olympics are segregated for misbehaving
psyops.scored_claim: A viral video, posted on X on Feb 12 and elsewhere, using a doctored CBC report with an AI voiceover to claim Ukrainian athletes were housed 'as far away as possible' from others because they 'behaved inappropriately' at Paris 2024; plus Russian Telegram videos claiming Ukrainian refugees were protesting the Games.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The video falsely carried CBC branding. CBC's fact-check, cited by EBU, found the original clip was replaced by an AI-generated one 16 seconds in; the real clip was posted on CBC's TikTok on Feb 4. The accounts that shared it had no sourcing.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Euronews: 'no credible reports' suggest Ukrainian athletes are housed separately, and the real CBC report by Adrienne Arsenault makes no mention of Ukrainian refugees. EBU found no reports that Ukrainian athletes were accused of misconduct in Paris 2024.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: Wording such as 'behaved inappropriately and caused conflicts' paints a group as troublemakers; the Telegram video called the Games an 'extravagant expense' ignoring Ukraine.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The claim omits that the real report was about the Olympic village in general, and that protests in Italy were by anti-ICE, anti-Olympics-cost and pro-Palestinian groups, not Ukrainians (Euronews).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: A tribal-resentment hook against a nationality; the posts are not graphic.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Euronews describes a 'large-scale campaign propagated by Russian Telegram channels'. Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation called the efforts 'coordinated' from Russian networks; the Centre is a Ukrainian government body, so that attribution comes from an interested party.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: Russia is banned from the Games, and the reported targets are its adversary's athletes; attribution to Russian networks rests on Euronews' and Ukraine's Centre's reporting, which I could not independently verify.

target_audience.text: Western social-media audiences, especially those sceptical of support for Ukraine and Italian and international viewers of the Games, with Ukrainian athletes and refugees as the targets.

confidence.reason: Euronews and EBU agree on the doctored clip and the lack of reports; I did not open CBC's own fact-check. The attribution to Russian networks rests on Euronews, Ukraine's Centre and a BBC Verify headline seen only as an excerpt.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: a real CBC report was replaced mid-clip with an AI-generated segment that blames Ukrainian athletes, and the fake spread under CBC's branding.
psyops.summary: As the Winter Olympics ran, fake and doctored videos claimed Ukrainian athletes were segregated for misbehaving and that Ukrainian refugees were protesting the Games. amplification.label: documented

psyops.headline: AI video 'shows Iran sinking the USS Abraham Lincoln' after the IRGC claimed it hit the carrier with four ballistic missiles

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: The Instagram post was viewed over 3.6 million times and shared over 66,000 times; the Facebook copy was shared over 200 times. The AI label was visible only on mobile.

incentive.label: documented for the IRGC claim; speculation for the account
incentive.note: The IRGC has a clear wartime incentive to claim a hit. AFP says the account looks to have been rebranded for an Iran focus, and X announced a revenue-sharing policy change on Mar 3 over AI war videos, which suggests a monetisation incentive (speculation).

target_audience.text: Arabic-, English- and Hindi-language social media users following the Iran war, and audiences inclined to believe US setbacks.

confidence.reason: I read the AFP Fact Check in full.

psyops.headline: FactChecking Trump's Prime-Time Address on Iran
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's April 1 address claims that before the U.S. attack Iran was 'right at the doorstep' of a nuclear bomb, would 'soon have had missiles that could reach the American homeland', and that he turned a 'dead and crippled' economy into the 'strongest in history' with 'no inflation' and '$18 trillion' of investment.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The 'obliterated' claim has some support: DNI Gabbard told Congress on March 18 that the strikes 'obliterated' Iran's enrichment program (FactCheck.org). But the 'doorstep of a bomb' claim cites no document, and Gabbard said only the president can decide what is an 'imminent threat'.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: FactCheck.org found the claims contradicted by data. The White House's own website puts investment at $10.5 trillion, not $18 trillion. Arms-control experts said a bomb was not 'imminent'. Real GDP grew 2.1% in 2025 versus 2.8% in 2024 (BEA), and unemployment was 4.4% in February (BLS).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Dead and crippled country', 'a nuclear weapon like nobody's ever seen before' and 'no inflation' are loaded phrases. CPI inflation was 2.4% in February, and the Cleveland Fed projected 3% for March (FactCheck.org).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Left out: a 2025 DIA report put an Iranian ICBM no earlier than 2035 (FactCheck.org); about 400 kg of 60% enriched uranium was already buried near Isfahan, which complicates the 'obliterated' line; and the U.S. has led world oil and gas output since 2013 and 2009, before Trump's leadership.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: A fear hook about a bomb and missiles reaching the American homeland, used to justify a war already a month old. The wording is vague ('soon', 'doorstep') rather than purely emotional.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: FactCheck.org notes the missile-range claim was nearly the same as in the Feb. 24 State of the Union, so these lines are repeated rather than newly sourced. No sign of coordinated third-party amplification was found.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The source is the commander in chief defending a war in its sixth week, so the speaker benefits directly from the justification being believed. That is a documented incentive; intent is an inference.

target_audience.text: U.S. voters and Congress whose support for the Iran war and its costs is in question, and a base receptive to the 'strongest economy' line. Foreign audiences are also addressed as a deterrent.

confidence.reason: I read FactCheck.org in full. NBC, PolitiFact and AP are search-index extracts only (AP fetch timed out). Some claims are opinion ('Obama deal', which FactCheck.org marks as such), and Gabbard's testimony partly backs the 'obliterated' claim.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: the same threat claims (imminent bomb, missiles reaching the U.S.) were repeated from the Feb. 24 State of the Union although arms-control experts disputed them, and the $18 trillion figure is contradicted by the White House's own $10.5 trillion. The mechanism is repetition of disputed threat claims plus an inflated statistic.
psyops.summary: Trump addressed the nation on April 1, a month into the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, and said the mission was 'getting very close' to done. FactCheck.org, PolitiFact and AP found several claims false or misleading, including investment totals, inflation, and the nearness of an Iranian bomb or long-range missile. The score applies to the address's claims, not to outlets' accurate reporting of it.
psyops.counter_argument: The claim that U.S. strikes badly damaged Iran's program is supported by the CIA director's June 2025 statement and by Gabbard's testimony. 'Doorstep' is vague, and Gabbard said Iran intended to rebuild.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented): on April 7 Trump suspended the threatened attack for two weeks and Iran accepted a two-week ceasefire (AP). The fact-check findings themselves were not changed by later events in the sources I read.

sourcing.note: The threat is the president's own Truth Social post, quoted identically by BBC, TIME, the Guardian and Al Jazeera, so the existence and wording of the claim are firmly sourced.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: The post exists. Whether the deadline is real is not checkable: BBC and AP document that earlier deadlines (March 21, March 28, April 6) were each extended, and on April 7 this one was suspended too.

framing.label: documented

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The post omits that the three previous deadlines passed without action (BBC). TIME notes that power-plant strikes would hit hospitals, water treatment and food supply, which the post does not mention.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: A threat of civilian infrastructure strikes ('hell'); Trump told the WSJ he was not concerned about civilian impact because 'they want us to do it' (Al Jazeera).

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: The same 'hell' and 'obliterate the power plants' threat recurs through March and April (BBC, AP), a repeated escalation script. I found no evidence of outside coordination.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The source is a party to the war, and the threat doubles as negotiating leverage while he said a deal was likely. That the threat is leverage is an inference.

psyops.headline: Trump announces 2-week Iran ceasefire after he'd warned 'a whole civilization will die tonight'
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's April 7 post that 'a whole civilization will die tonight' unless Iran agreed to reopen Hormuz, and his claim that a 'final' 8 p.m. deadline was firm, which he reversed about 90 minutes before it expired.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: Primary source is the president's own Truth Social posts, quoted in full by NBC, which also cites the Fox/Baier relay and his Monday news conference.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: The words are documented. Whether he meant it is unverifiable: Fox's Baier relayed that '8 p.m. is happening' that morning, then he suspended the attack that evening, after Pakistan's PM and army chief asked him to wait.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'A whole civilization will die tonight' and 'every bridge in Iran will be decimated... every power plant... burning, exploding' (Trump's news conference quoted by NBC) are maximal, existential wording. NBC calls it his 'most extreme public rhetoric' of the war.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The post did not mention that the deadline had already been extended several times (NBC), and it framed a binary outcome; the outcome was a ceasefire on terms Trump called 'workable' (Iran's 10-point plan).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: A threat to civilian infrastructure drew war-crimes warnings from Democratic senators, international-law experts (Kenneth Roth), and rare dissent from Sen. Ron Johnson (R) and MTG, which shows the fear hook was itself the story.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: NBC reports the threat was repeated across posts, a press conference and phone interviews in the same 48 hours, and the official Senate Republican account (run by Cotton's staff) amplified a matching message.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The speaker is a party to the war, using the threat as leverage ahead of Islamabad talks. Senator Schumer called it 'ridiculous bluster'; that reading is opinion.

target_audience.text: Iran's leadership (coercive signaling), allied governments and oil markets watching the Hormuz deadline, and a domestic audience; Pakistan's mediators were the practical audience.

confidence.reason: I read NBC's full article, which quotes the post and the reversal. NPR, Reuters and CNBC returned matching headlines in search; Reuters and NPR could not be opened. Intent is an inference.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: a maximal existential threat was issued hours before a 'final' deadline and withdrawn about 90 minutes before it expired after mediator requests. The mechanism is a coercive-threat/reversal cycle, with fear as the hook. Whether it was bluff or real is speculation.
psyops.summary: On the morning of April 7 Trump posted that 'a whole civilization will die tonight'. That evening he announced a two-week ceasefire contingent on reopening Hormuz, citing requests from Pakistan's leaders. NBC reports the threat prompted denunciations from Democrats and rare criticism from some Republicans. The score applies to the threat's framing and its reliability, not to NBC's accurate reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: The threat was not hidden or deceptive about what he might do, and it coincided with an actual diplomatic opening: Iran submitted a 10-point plan and talks began in Islamabad. A reasonable reading is that it worked as leverage.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented): CNN reported marathon U.S.-Iran talks in Islamabad led by VP Vance on April 11 that ended without agreement, chiefly over Iran's nuclear program, and Al-Monitor reported the U.S. would extend the ceasefire indefinitely though Iran's acceptance was unclear.

psyops.headline: Fact-checking falsehoods after shooting in hotel hosting correspondents' dinner Trump attended
psyops.scored_claim: X and Instagram posts claiming the April 25 Correspondents' Dinner shooting was staged or a 'false flag': Leavitt's 'shots fired' remark, a Fox reporter 'cut off', and a mentalist's card as a 'signal'.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The posts rely on clipped video and inference, e.g. 'What did Karoline Leavitt know?', not on any document or witness.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: PolitiFact found Leavitt's remark referred to Trump's planned jokes. Fox's Aishah Hasnie said her call dropped for poor ballroom cell service, and the card-holder was mentalist Oz Pearlman mid-trick. Snopes found no viable evidence of staging but left the Fox cut-off claim unrated because it could not verify why the line dropped.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'HOLY SH*T... Fox cut one of their reporters off as they seemed to indicate the shooting was a pre-planned false flag' is built to read as a smoking gun.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Context was removed: the 'shots fired' line came in a joking pre-event Fox interview about Trump's speech; the Hasnie clip was cut mid-sentence by signal loss; the suspect was tackled, not shot, per Metropolitan Police interim chief Jeffery Carroll.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Shock and distrust hooks, in a context where Trump had survived two earlier assassination attempts, which PolitiFact notes.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Multiple X posts and an Instagram repost circulated the same clips with near-identical 'false flag' framings, per PolitiFact, Snopes and NBC's 'conspiracy theories swirl' report.

incentive.label: speculation
incentive.note: Likely engagement or partisan motives; PolitiFact does not identify the posters' intent.

target_audience.text: Social-media audiences distrustful of the administration or of media, and audiences primed to see staged events (inference).

confidence.reason: I read PolitiFact and Snopes in full; AFP and NBC were search extracts. Snopes itself left one sub-claim unrated, which I preserved.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: clipped video and out-of-context remarks (Leavitt's joke, a dropped phone call, a mentalist's card) were presented as proof of a staged attack. The mechanism is decontextualized clips plus a leading question. PolitiFact also documented an honest error by a CNN reporter ('confirmed dead') corrected within about 10 minutes, which fed the confusion.
psyops.summary: On April 25 a gunman charged a security checkpoint at the Washington Hilton during the dinner; a Secret Service agent was hit in a vest. Within hours, posts claimed the shooting was staged. PolitiFact and Snopes traced the claims to misread clips. The score applies to those posts, not to the fact-checks.
psyops.counter_argument: Snopes says it cannot be certain the Fox call dropped from signal rather than being cut, which is why it left that claim unrated. Nothing in the sources supports staging, but Snopes' caution is fair.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented): the suspect was charged on April 27 with attempting to assassinate the president (AP and DOJ pages in search results; I did not open them).
gaps: DOJ and AP pages were read only as search extracts.

psyops.headline: Trump claims Iran is in 'state of collapse,' wants Strait of Hormuz reopened
psyops.outlet: New York Post (with Reuters, AP, DW)
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's Truth Social post: 'Iran has just informed us that they are in a "State of Collapse". They want us to "Open the Hormuz Strait" as soon as possible.'

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The only source is Trump's own post. Reuters said it was unclear how Iran communicated this or whether Tehran responded.

verifiability.label: disputed
verifiability.note: No independent confirmation. AP reported Iran's actual offer: reopen Hormuz after the U.S. lifts its blockade, while postponing nuclear talks. The NY Post says earlier claimed concessions (e.g., handing over 'nuclear dust') had not panned out.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: Scare quotes around 'State of Collapse' and 'Open the Hormuz Strait' present them as Iran's words.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Omits that Iran's proposal was conditional on ending the blockade (AP). Also, a Trump claim that Iran's oil lines would 'explode' in about three days had not been independently confirmed (NY Post).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: No fear or outrage hook; the post is a pressure statement.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Same message from Rubio ('deeply fractured internally') and a series of earlier Trump claims of imminent deals (NY Post), a consistent administration line.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The source is a party to the war, using the claim to pressure Tehran and justify the blockade; that is its documented position, though motive is an inference.

target_audience.text: Iran's leadership and negotiators (pressure), oil markets, and a U.S. public tiring of the war, which is an inference.

confidence.reason: I read the NY Post article in full. Reuters and AP extracts support the framing. I could not verify any Iranian communication.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: a private-communication claim with no corroboration, contradicted in emphasis by Iran's public conditions (AP). The mechanism is an unverifiable quoted concession used for leverage; the 'collapse' itself is speculation.
psyops.summary: On April 28 Trump posted that Iran told the U.S. it was in a 'State of Collapse' and wanted Hormuz reopened. Reuters said it was unclear how Iran conveyed it. AP reported Iran's offer was conditional on the blockade ending. The score applies to the claim, not to outlets' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Iran's offer to reopen the strait does show it wants the standoff to end, and Rubio and Reuters describe internal fractures in leadership. Pressure from the blockade is real (48 ships turned back by May 2, per Newsweek extract).
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented): on May 3 Trump launched 'Project Freedom' to escort stranded ships and Iran warned it would attack U.S. forces (Newsweek extract).
gaps: Reuters and AP pages could not be opened; extracts only.

psyops.headline: Judge blocks Trump's White House media ban, orders access to be restored
psyops.scored_claim: The administration's stated rationale that banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House protects national security.
psyops.selection_reason: First psyop of the week: single-source claim of fact with an identifiable source incentive (see factors).

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The security claim rested on Justice Department letters sent on Tuesday 9/22, after the ban and after the lawsuit (Reuters), and on Defense Department declarations. The judge said those officials had 'no direct knowledge of how reporters operate in the White House' (BBC).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Judge Kelly: 'The record lacks factual support for defendants' contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will in fact protect national security' (TRO, quoted by Reuters and BBC).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: The letters cited reporting that 'threatened national security and/or spread falsehoods', blending a security claim with a content complaint (TRO). Trump's post said the outlets 'shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES' (Reuters). The judge said the stories cited 'are routine' (NBC).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The administration named the specific articles it objected to, so they were not hidden. It left out context that NBC supplies: AP and CNBC ran the same background-briefing story under the same attribution and were not banned. Trump's 9/18 announcement did not mention security (TRO).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Tribal and fear hooks: 'FAKE NEWS' and 'FICTION and LIES' in Trump's posts (NBC, Reuters), and a security label that implies danger without evidence.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: The security rationale first appeared in the post-suit letters and court filings of 9/22 (Reuters, BBC). It was repeated in later social media posts (court opinion of 10/13, hindsight).

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The source is the government, which gains in court from a security label: the TRO notes that review of the executive's national-security determinations is 'highly deferential'. Motive is an inference.

target_audience.text: Federal courts, which defer more to national-security claims, and a public and base receptive to the 'fake news' framing.

confidence.reason: I read the 9/24 TRO and the 10/13 preliminary-injunction opinion directly, and Reuters, BBC and NBC agree. The judge's findings are preliminary ('likely to succeed') and the government disputes them.

psyops.mechanism: Documented: the security rationale appears only after the ban and the lawsuit. The 9/18 announcement cited 'fake news', and the TRO found the record lacked factual support that the ban protects national security. The court later called it 'merely a post-hoc justification'.
psyops.summary: Trump announced on 9/18 that he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, citing 'fake news'. After the outlets sued, the government defended the ban as protecting national security. On 9/24 Judge Kelly ordered access restored for 14 days and found no factual support for the security claim. Reuters, BBC and NBC reported this accurately; the score applies to the claim, not to their reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: The judge called national security a 'weighty' interest and wrote that his ruling should not be read to suggest Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are 'unfounded'. NBC notes some cited articles concerned munitions stockpiles. The findings are preliminary and the government disputes them.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented, not knowable on 9/24): on 10/13 Judge Kelly granted a preliminary injunction (Doc. 50), finding the outlets likely to succeed on due process and two First Amendment claims. He wrote that 'national security' appears to have been 'merely a post-hoc justification for the decision'.
gaps: Trump's 9/18 Truth Social post and the Justice Department's 9/22 letters were not opened directly. They are quoted from the TRO, Reuters and NBC.

The TRO text was read from a third-party mirror (brynodc.com) of court document 24 in case 1:26-cv-03287-TJK, not from the court's own system. The caption, docket number and 09/24/26 filing date match the 10/13 opinion's description.
The AP original was blocked and the Reuters original is paywalled. Reuters text was read through Yahoo News.

psyops.headline: Trump administration lowers fuel economy standards, critics say at a significant environmental cost
psyops.scored_claim: DOT's and the White House's framing of the 9/28 fuel-economy rollback as ending an 'illegal mandate' and making cars $1,300 cheaper.
psyops.selection_reason: First psyop of the week: single-source claim of fact with an identifiable source incentive (see factors).

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The headline savings ($1,300 lower average new-vehicle price; $138 billion in consumer savings over five years) come from DOT itself (AP, Roll Call, USA Today). The 892-page final rule is the primary document, but I could not open it.

verifiability.label: disputed
verifiability.note: NHTSA's own regulatory analysis shows drivers spending about $1,624 more on fuel over a vehicle's life (USA Today). The Environmental Defense Fund cites about $1,600 more (Roll Call). The sticker-price estimate is not independently confirmed.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: DOT titled the rule 'Freedom Means Affordable Cars' and Secretary Duffy called it ending an 'illegal mandate'. AP notes that Trump 'falsely calls' it an EV 'mandate' and that no federal policy has mandated EV sales. Trump's preview post called past cars 'Environmental Monsters' (Roll Call).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: DOT's headline figures leave out the roughly $1,624 lifetime fuel-cost increase in NHTSA's own analysis (USA Today). DOT's oil-use comparison is against 2024, while AP notes the prior standards were estimated to save 14 billion gallons of gasoline by 2050.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Appeals to family affordability ('American dream') alongside the 'Environmental Monsters' jab: a mild identity hook. Facts still do most of the work.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Trump previewed the rule on Truth Social on Saturday 9/26 and DOT released it on Monday 9/28, an ordinary rollout. Automaker statements echo 'market realities' (AP, USA Today), but I found no coordinated push.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The agency announcing the savings wrote the rule. Automakers that gain flexibility (the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, Ford, GM, Stellantis) praised it (AP). AP puts it against gas at $4.47 a gallon and the midterms. Motive is an inference.

target_audience.text: Car buyers and households worried about vehicle prices and the cost of living, plus the administration's base and automakers.

confidence.reason: AP, Roll Call, USA Today and Carbon Brief agree on the figures. I could not open the DOT press release or the NHTSA analysis (blocked), so the numbers are read through outlets that quote them.

psyops.summary: On Monday 9/28 DOT released a final rule resetting CAFE standards to about 34.9 mpg for model year 2031, down from the 50.4 mpg projected under the Biden-era rule. It said the change would cut the average new-vehicle price by $1,300. NHTSA's own analysis shows drivers paying about $1,624 more for fuel. The outlets reported both. The score applies to the administration's framing, not to the outlets' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: DOT did publish the fuel-cost increase in its regulatory analysis, so the figure was disclosed rather than hidden. Whether regulation or the market should set fuel-economy targets is a legitimate policy dispute, and automakers publicly backed the change.
psyops.hindsight_note: This window is under three weeks old. I verified no later outcome yet (AP reports the Sierra Club 'vowed to fight the rule').
gaps: The DOT press release and the NHTSA regulatory analysis were not opened (HTTP 403 to automated access). Figures come from AP, Roll Call and USA Today, which quote them.
The AP original was blocked and the Reuters article is paywalled. AP text was read through PBS News.
The Washington Post's view that analysts 'doubt' the price cut is known only secondhand through Carbon Brief.

psyops.headline: Trump says Russia, Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire'
psyops.scored_claim: Trump's claim, posted on Truth Social on 10/11, that Russia and Ukraine 'both agreed' to an immediate energy ceasefire.
psyops.selection_reason: First psyop of the week: single-source claim of fact with an identifiable source incentive (see factors).

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The only source for 'Both parties have agreed' is Trump's own Truth Social post. No document, terms, scope or start time were published. DW and NBC both report no immediate confirmation from Moscow.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Zelenskyy told Axios within minutes it was 'news for me' (DW). The Kremlin said only that 'contacts are ongoing' (NBC). No second independent source confirmed that an agreement existed.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Effective immediately... Do not break it!' reads as settled fact plus an enforcement order, while the outlets mostly attributed it ('Trump says', 'Trump claims').

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The post gives no definition of 'energy infrastructure' and no terms for either side. It also leaves out context that NBC and DW report: it followed the 10/09 diesel deal, it came weeks before the 11/03 midterms, and NBC notes a similar announcement a month earlier that neither side confirmed.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: The post is terse. Apart from the imperative 'Do not break it!' it carries no fear or outrage hook.

amplification.label: disputed
amplification.note: The announcement came a day after Trump called for Ukraine to 'get a new leader' (NBC) and two days after the diesel deal. The quote was reproduced identically across outlets, which is normal for a presidential post. I found no evidence of a coordinated account push.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The source is also the party that benefits. DW and NBC report that Trump needs lower fuel prices before the midterms and has blamed Ukraine's refinery strikes, not the Iran war, for high diesel prices. A truce halting those strikes would serve that goal. Motive is an inference.

target_audience.text: U.S. voters worried about fuel prices ahead of the 11/03 midterms, and Trump's domestic base. Moscow and Kyiv are secondary audiences, pressured to comply publicly.

confidence.reason: What Trump posted, Zelenskyy's reaction and the lack of confirmation from Moscow are documented by three in-window outlets. I did not open the Truth Social post or the AP and Reuters originals. Motive is inference.

psyops.summary: On Sunday 10/11 Trump posted that an 'ENERGY CEASEFIRE' was in effect and that 'both parties have agreed'. Ukraine's president said it was news to him. Moscow did not confirm. No terms were published. Coverage in the window was accurate and attributed; the score applies to the claim, not to the outlets' reporting.
psyops.counter_argument: Zelenskyy had himself offered on ABC's 'This Week' the same day to stop hitting Russian refineries if Russia stopped hitting Ukraine's grid (NBC). Trump's post may have been a public attempt to bring both sides to a deal they were each already signalling. An unconfirmed announcement is not proof of deception.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window closed (documented, not knowable on 10/11): Ukrainian officials said Russia kept striking energy sites in the hours after the post and on Monday morning, including near Kharkiv (NBC; Reuters text via The Business Standard). The Kremlin said 'contacts are ongoing' and rejected a 60-day truce (Reuters via The Business Standard; BBC). On 10/12 Trump said 'They agreed because I said they agreed' (RFE/RL). By 10/13 RFE/RL reported that neither side had confirmed the truce.
gaps: The Truth Social post itself was not retrieved. The wording comes from DW, The Guardian and NBC, which quote it identically.

The AP and Reuters originals could not be opened (AP blocks automated access; Reuters is paywalled). Wire content was checked through DW (credits AFP and Reuters) and The Business Standard (Reuters text).
The Axios interview with Zelenskyy was not opened (blocked). The quote is taken from DW, NBC and The Guardian.
No Kremlin primary transcript was opened. Peskov's statements are known only through NBC, BBC and Reuters.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: Official statements are 'tersely worded' (AP); the unverified plague framing was spread by unconfirmed media reports.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Russia reported 'no biosecurity incidents', contrary to early media reports, without detail on the tests or lab records.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Official statements are terse and unemotional; the outlets' own reporting is restrained.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Early media reports and later official statements diverged, but I found no evidence of a coordinated push; Trump also asked for information (NPR).

incentive.label: documented
incentive.note: Russia's authorities have an incentive to downplay a possible lab accident; the early rumours' sources are unnamed.

target_audience.text: International health and security audiences; Russian public. Inference.

confidence.reason: CNN, NPR and WHO text (via search) are consistent; WHO's own report and AP not opened directly.

psyops.summary: Russia gave shifting accounts and no confirmed cause of death; WHO says risk cannot be fully assessed. The score applies to the completeness and consistency of Russia's account, not to outlets' reporting of it.
psyops.counter_argument: Russia's testing and contact quarantine may be accurate; the absence of detail does not show concealment.

psyops.headline: Two container ships sink near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacks
psyops.scored_claim: The IRGC's statement, quoted by Iranian state television, that a cargo ship (apparently the GFS Pride) sank on 10/14 after hitting a naval mine while on an 'illegal and dangerous route' through the Strait of Hormuz.
psyops.selection_reason: Official claim of fact contradicted by the maritime security reporting body, with an identifiable source incentive.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The only source for the mine account is the IRGC, through Iranian state television (The Guardian). No ship name, position or evidence of a mine was given in the statement as reported.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: The Joint Maritime Information Center's 10/15 advisory lists the GFS Pride as 'struck by an unknown projectile' on 10/13 and says of the IRGC's 10/14 mine claim: 'there is no substantiation to this claim.' UKMTO also reported both sinking ships as hit by unidentified projectiles (The Guardian).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Illegal and dangerous route' puts the blame on the ship for using a lane Iran has not approved, while the U.S. military has been guiding ships along a route nearer Oman (The Guardian).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The statement leaves out the projectile strike UKMTO reported the day before, and the five attacks on shipping in the previous 48 hours that UKMTO logged.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: The message works as a warning to other ships; it is a threat more than an emotional appeal.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Two Iranian officials told Reuters (quoted by The Guardian) that the new tactics aim to 'frustrate' efforts to lower oil prices before the U.S. midterms. A run of earlier IRGC mine claims since July was rejected by CENTCOM, which in August called one 'disinformation' (gCaptain, published after the window).

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The source is the party accused of the attacks. A mine on an 'unauthorized' route shifts responsibility away from Iran and deters ships from the U.S.-guided lane. Motive is inference.

target_audience.text: Shipping companies, insurers and crews deciding whether to use the U.S.-guided route; secondarily U.S. voters facing fuel prices before the 11/03 midterms. Inference.

confidence.reason: The JMIC advisory (primary) and The Guardian were opened and agree. The IRGC statement itself was read only as quoted by The Guardian; motive is inference.

psyops.mechanism: Deflection: a ship that the JMIC and UKMTO record as hit by an unknown projectile is recast as the victim of a mine on an 'illegal' route, putting the blame on the ship and warning others off the U.S.-guided lane. The JMIC states the claim has no substantiation (documented).
psyops.summary: On 10/14 the IRGC said a container ship sank after hitting a mine on an 'illegal' route. The multinational JMIC advisory records the GFS Pride as hit by an unknown projectile on 10/13 and says the mine claim has no substantiation. The score applies to the IRGC's claim, not to The Guardian's reporting of it.
psyops.counter_argument: Iran has said it mined the unauthorized lanes, and the JMIC itself warns mariners to watch for mining activity in the area. A mine strike is possible in principle; the advisory says only that the claim is unsubstantiated, not that it is disproved.
psyops.hindsight_note: After the window (documented, not knowable on 10/14): on 10/18 the IRGC said another tanker hit a mine (Middle East Eye), and on 10/20 gCaptain reported the JMIC's 10/18 advisory saying the IRGC's 10/17 claim of two supertankers hitting mines had 'no substantiation'.
gaps: The IRGC statement and the Iranian state television broadcast were not opened; the wording comes from The Guardian.
The Reuters report quoting two Iranian officials was read only as quoted by The Guardian.

The JMIC advisory and The Guardian disagree on the Cape Dao: The Guardian says it sank, while the advisory says 'her status remains disputed, but she is not sunk'. The score does not rest on the Cape Dao.

psyops.headline: Out of context: How a video of Maricopa County election workers fueled a false election fraud narrative
psyops.outlet: Center for an Informed Public (University of Washington)
psyops.scored_claim: Viral X posts claiming a video shows two Maricopa County election workers doing something nefarious by inserting flash drives into computers at the ballot tabulation center late at night.
psyops.selection_reason: Viral election-fraud claim built on a real video, with a documented amplification pattern ahead of the midterms.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The video was released by the 'election watchdog' group We The People Alliance USA as an 'exclusive video' 'obtained by our source', with no named source (CIP).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Maricopa County officials confirmed the two people were county election employees finishing a routine software update before a long weekend (CIP).

framing.label: documented
framing.note: The posts frame normal work as suspicious, add a 'toddler in tow' detail, and name one employee who was at the center of earlier 2020 'rigged election' claims (CIP).

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The posts leave out what the workers were doing and the county's explanation; the CIP notes the named employee has never been found guilty of the earlier claims.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: The appeal is mistrust more than fear or outrage, with a named individual as the target.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: Kari Lake (3.1M followers) reposted it, drawing 440.3K views, and The SCIF's quote post helped drive it to 35,000 posts within three days (CIP).

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The accounts pushing it have promoted 'rigged election' claims before, and the claim serves that narrative weeks before the 11/03 midterms. Motive is inference.

target_audience.text: Voters already inclined to distrust election results, especially in Arizona, ahead of the 11/03 midterms. Inference.

confidence.reason: The CIP analysis was opened and quotes the county's explanation; the original X posts and the county statement were not opened directly.

psyops.mechanism: Decontextualized video: routine election work recast as tampering, with a named employee targeted, then amplified by large accounts (Kari Lake, The SCIF) to 35,000 posts in three days. The county's explanation and the spread are documented by the CIP.
psyops.summary: A late-night video of two Maricopa County election workers was spread on X as evidence of tampering. The county says they were doing a routine software update. The CIP documents how a small group's post reached 35,000 posts through large accounts. The score applies to the viral claim, not to the CIP's analysis.
psyops.counter_argument: The posters did not invent the video, and election workers handling computers late at night can look odd without context. Asking questions about it is not itself manipulation.
gaps: The video was first posted on 10/09 (week 41); it is scored in week 42 because its spread and the CIP analysis (10/15) fall in this week.
The original X posts and Maricopa County's own statement were not opened; their content comes from the CIP.

psyops.headline: In North Carolina and other states, a ballot isn't disqualified if a poll worker marks it
psyops.scored_claim: Viral posts (X, TikTok, Facebook, texts) claiming that if a poll worker writes anything on your ballot 'your ballot could be disqualified' and you should request a new one.
psyops.selection_reason: Recycled viral election rumor debunked by officials in several states during early voting.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The text rests on 'a very reliable good friend of a family member' who 'just finished POLL worker training' (KVIA). No named source.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Election officials in North Carolina, New Mexico, Florida, Illinois and Tennessee said it is false (PolitiFact, KVIA, NBC News). Some states, including North Carolina and Texas, require poll workers to mark ballots.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'VOTERS BEWARE!!' and 'please, please pass this on' are urgency cues; the rest is phrased as helpful advice.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Leaves out that marks do not disqualify a ballot and that some marking is required by law. North Carolina's board says the posts 'have been circulating for several years'; PolitiFact debunked an identical claim before 2024.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Fear of losing your vote is the hook, and it asks readers to act at the polling place.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: The same wording appears across states and platforms: the New Mexico post (KVIA) and the 10/12 Facebook post quoted by PolitiFact are near-identical copy-paste chain text.

incentive.label: speculation
incentive.note: No identified originator or beneficiary. The likely effect is distrust of poll workers and disputes at polling places.

target_audience.text: Early voters, especially those already wary of poll workers, in North Carolina, New Mexico, Florida and other states. Inference.

confidence.reason: PolitiFact and KVIA were opened and quote the posts and officials; the NBC News page was opened but only its opening paragraph was read.

psyops.mechanism: Copy-paste chain message with a fake insider source ('a very reliable good friend' who 'just finished poll worker training'), recycled since at least 2020 and spread with near-identical wording across states and platforms (documented by PolitiFact, KVIA and state officials).
psyops.summary: A chain message warning that poll worker marks will disqualify ballots spread across several states during early voting. Officials in at least five states said it is false; some states require such marks. The score applies to the viral claim, not to the fact-checkers.
psyops.counter_argument: Stray marks in the timing bars or ovals can stop a tabulator reading a ballot (PolitiFact), so the advice to ask about a marked ballot is not entirely baseless, and many sharers likely meant well.
gaps: The original posts were not opened; their wording comes from KVIA and PolitiFact.
The NBC News article was opened, but only its standfirst and first paragraph could be read.

psyops.scored_claim: X posts claiming hurricanes Isaias, Rachel and Simon were artificially engineered, with Isaias deliberately steered into Florida's Gulf Coast ('It is so painfully clear that the three hurricanes arriving at the same time are engineered', 10/13).
psyops.selection_reason: Viral conspiracy claim after three simultaneous storms, rebutted by meteorologists.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: Anonymous X posts; no data or document is cited beyond research images (AFP).

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: Meteorologists told AFP no human technology can create or steer storms of this size; an intense El Nino and other conditions explain them.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: 'Painfully clear' and 'artificially pumping chemical clouds' assert certainty without evidence; some posts read meaning into the storms' Biblical names.

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Visuals of marine cloud brightening research were lifted from Scottish and Australian university portals; the posts leave out that this research works on shallow clouds and cannot steer storms.

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: Distrust and fear of a hidden hand after storms that killed people in Florida and Mexico.

amplification.label: documented
amplification.note: AFP reports 'similar posts'; no coordination was shown.

incentive.label: speculation
incentive.note: No beneficiary identified; engagement and distrust of government are the likely drivers. Inference.

target_audience.text: Social media users primed for weather-control and anti-government conspiracy theories, especially in storm-hit Florida. Inference.

confidence.reason: AFP's text was read through a search excerpt; the page returned 403 to the box's curl. The original posts were not opened.

psyops.mechanism: Real research material used out of context: cloud-brightening visuals from university portals presented as proof that the storms were engineered (documented by AFP; experts quoted say storms cannot be created or steered).
psyops.summary: As three hurricanes hit North America in one weekend, X posts claimed they were engineered, using real cloud-brightening research images as 'proof'. Meteorologists told AFP that is impossible with current technology. The score applies to the viral posts, not to AFP.
psyops.counter_argument: Cloud seeding and cloud brightening research does exist, so the posts point at something real, and three near-simultaneous storms are unusual enough to invite questions.

verifiability.note: No independent confirmation; the Houthis denied any operation against Saudi territory that day (France 24, The Hindu).

framing.label: documented

omission.label: documented
omission.note: Launcher, intended target and evidence are all missing from the announcement (Military Ledger).

emotional.label: documented

amplification.label: documented

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation

psyops.headline: Turkish police raid opposition TV station, halting live broadcasts
psyops.scored_claim: The Istanbul Chief Prosecutor's Office's account that the 10/14 raid on Halk TV and the appointment of a state trustee (TMSF) were a financial-crimes case against chairman Cafer Mahiroglu for 'bribery, tender-rigging, and laundering of assets derived from crime'.
psyops.selection_reason: Official justification for a state takeover of a major opposition broadcaster.

sourcing.label: documented
sourcing.note: The prosecutor's office is named and cites MASAK financial data, confidential witness testimony and suspect statements (Hurriyet Daily News), but none of the evidence is public.

verifiability.label: documented
verifiability.note: No court has ruled; the allegations cannot be checked independently.

framing.label: documented
framing.note: The statement is legalistic; the loaded language comes from the opposition ('only dictators').

omission.label: documented
omission.note: The statement leaves out that a trustee halts the channel's live news: broadcasts were cut at 6:30 a.m. (Reuters via ThePrint). It also omits that this is the fifth major outlet put under a trustee, and that Tele1's news content was stripped after its takeover (BBC).

emotional.label: documented
emotional.note: No fear or outrage hook in the official account.

amplification.label: disputed
amplification.note: The Istanbul Bar Association noted the raid came hours before Ekrem Imamoglu was due to begin his defence in court (BBC). The timing may be coincidence.

incentive.label: documented incentive; motive is speculation
incentive.note: The government that benefits from silencing a critical channel controls the prosecutors who seized it; RSF says 90% of national media is under government control (BBC). Motive is inference.

target_audience.text: Turkish domestic audiences, and foreign governments the government wants to see the move as a corruption case rather than censorship. Inference.

confidence.reason: BBC, Reuters text (via ThePrint) and Hurriyet Daily News were opened and agree on the facts. The prosecutor's statement was not opened directly, and the merits of the corruption case are unknown.

psyops.summary: Police raided Halk TV, cut its live broadcasts and installed a state trustee, with prosecutors citing bribery and money laundering by its owner. The facts are well documented; the score applies to the official framing of the takeover as a purely financial case.
psyops.counter_argument: Mahiroglu had been under scrutiny before over public procurement, and a businessman's statements led to a separate inquiry (Hurriyet Daily News). The corruption allegations could be true even if the takeover also silences a critic.
gaps: The Istanbul Chief Prosecutor's Office statement was not opened; its content comes from Reuters (via ThePrint) and Hurriyet Daily News.
